title: Why the ECB Rate Hike Cycle Is Not Over
paragraphs: The European Central Bank faces an increasingly uncomfortable choice: risk tightening monetary policy too little as an extended energy shock threatens to entrench inflation, or tighten too much and amplify meaningful strains in sovereign bond markets.

Officials want to prevent the energy crisis from becoming embedded in the regional economy and have left open an option of a hike this week. But for now, the most likely outcome is a hold at the meeting concluding on Thursday, 29 October, with a 25-basis-point rate hike anticipated in December under a quarterly pace of hiking once fresh projections become available.

The Governing Council may begin laying the groundwork for such a December move in its communications this week, even if it stops short of any explicit commitment. The message being that the ECB remains data-dependent, but that the balance of risks has shifted towards inflation running hotter than previously anticipated.

With the Iran war prolonged and energy markets edging beyond even an ECB adverse scenario presented last month, the likelihood of rates being raised above neutral, and staying there for some period after, is becoming harder to dismiss. Further tightening next year can no longer be ruled out.
Inflation's Second Round Is the ECB's Real Concern
The crucial question is if elevated energy prices may increasingly affect domestic price-setting, wage negotiations and inflation expectations.

Headline inflation rose to 3.8% year over year last month (Figure 1) – nearly double a central-bank objective. This is even as core inflation nudged up only one tenth to 2.5%. Nevertheless, the longer headline inflation stays elevated, the harder it becomes to dismiss second-round effects that could make an external shock considerably harder to reverse.

As I said on Bloomberg – for the ECB, an inflation overshoot is today a far greater medium-run risk than an undershoot. The nominal neutral rate — the rate consistent with the economy operating at its potential without monetary policy pushing demand in either direction — may also be drifting slightly higher from a starting point around 2% as persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty reshape the policy backdrop.

The euro should furthermore be watched closely. Its depreciation (Figure 2) adds to the inflationary impulse by making energy and other imports more expensive – amplifying inflationary dynamics and strengthening the case for monetary tightening.
